senses: Capable of, or suitable for, being hugged.
ety: From hug + -able.
examples: How high? Real high 'cause I'm just so fly / A young lovable, huggable type of guy
Claud was glad to oblige, since Gabbie is an extremely huggable girl.
Moreover, this need often manifests itself in the young child's selection of a cuddly or huggable doll or stuffed animal, called a transitional object by child psychologists.

senses: Morally objectionable; sinful, wicked.
Grossly unfair or unjust.
ety: From iniquity + -ous (suffix forming adjectives indicating the presence of a quality in any degree (typically an abundance)).
examples: Are you aware, sir, that we have gone to enormous expense to resist this iniquitous attempt of yours?
I've had it. That's it George! For one year now, I've been providing X-rated entertainment and you reciprocate with PG! It's an iniquitous arrangement!

senses: A horseman or cavalryman, especially a German one, associated with the wars of the 16th and 17th centuries.
ety: From Middle Dutch ruter, rutter, variants of ruiter, from Middle French routier (“mercenary soldier”), corresponding to route + ier; see rout.
examples: Such a regiment of rutters / Never defied men braver

senses: Tending to hug; affectionate in a physical way.
ety: From hug + -y.
examples: Gordy, who looks sort of like a bear cub, only not cute, is a very huggy person.
I wasn't typically a huggy person, but I knew better than to argue with anyone in Bones's genetic line.
Sonia is an affectionate but not very huggy woman.

senses: Synonym of update, especially in reference to Italian scholarship or (Roman Catholicism) the updating of doctrine and practices by the Roman Catholic Church as part of the 1962–1965 Second Vatican Council.
ety: From Italian aggiornamento (“updating; adjournment”), from aggiornare (“update; postpone”) + -mento (“-ment”), from French ajourner (“to postpone”), q.v. Doublet of adjournment.
examples: Buonocore's comments and bibliographical aggiornamenti are again exemplary.
Aggiornamento with the increasingly truculent magistrates was a major plank of Choiseul's recovery strategy for the state.

senses: A drinking game wherein players must remember personal hand signs while being distracted by others banging on a table.
A short rope for beating disobedient sled dogs.
A strong adherent to a religion or ideology.
A track with a thumping beat.
ety: From thump + -er.
examples: But in spite of the antics of its Bible thumpers and its boobocracy, my father was unable to stay mad at the United States for long.

This late-1979 disco thumper is set to a driving beat with a memorable refrain that proved so enduring that American icon Madonna sampled it for her 2005 hit 'Hung Up', from her album Confessions on a Dance Floor.

senses: Someone who has retired from active working.
ety: From retire + -ee.
examples: He has been a retiree since 2001.

senses: Synonym of hundredweight, 100 or 112 English or American pounds.
Various other similar units of weight in other systems.
An unofficial metric unit equal to 100 kg.
ety: Late Middle English, from Anglo-Norman quintal, from Middle French quintal, from Old French and Medieval Latin quintale and quintallus (“various medieval hundredweights”), from Arabic قِنْطَار (qinṭār, “100 rottols”), from Classical Syriac ܩܰܢܛܺܝܪܳܐ (qanṭīrā) and ܩܰܢܛܺܝܢܳܪܳܐ (qanṭīnārā), from Byzantine Greek κεντηνάριον (kentēnárion), from Latin centēnārium (“100 Roman pounds”), from the neuter of centēnārius (“having 100 things”). Use for various non-English units, borrowed from French quintal, Spanish quintal, Portuguese quintal, etc. The apparent relation to quint- (“five, fivefold”) and -a
examples: In one import license alone, the merchant in question was instructed to bring in 13,000 quintals of alum, which, snapped up by industries in England and the Low Countries, would yield the king a cool £8,666 13s 4d.

senses: To change from a liquid to solid state, perhaps due to cold; called to freeze in nontechnical usage.
To coagulate, make curdled or semi-solid such as gel or jelly.
To make rigid or immobile.
To become congealed, solidify.
ety: From Middle English congelen, from Middle French congeler, from Latin congelare, cognate with Portuguese and Spanish congelar.
examples: We must act before opposition to our plans congeals.

senses: A considerable lump, scoop, or quantity of something, especially soft food.
ety: From earlier East Anglian dialectal dallop (“patch, tuft (of grass, etc.)”), of unknown origin. Compare dialectal Norwegian dolp (“lump”).
examples: Each pancake comes with a dollop of suspiciously soft butter in a tiny plastic cup.

Although I was short and stubby, and could hardly manage a good serve or a great smash, what I lacked in height and strength I made up with dollops of enthusiasm and even managed it to the victorious throw-ball team.

senses: The act or process of endearing, of causing (something or someone) to be loved or to be the object of affection.
The state or characteristic of being endeared.
An expression of affection.
ety: From endear + -ment.
examples: Every step of that walk led Jeff deeper into an excursion of endearment. It was amazingly true that he trod beside her an acknowledged friend, a secret lover.
He could not forget the fond and earnest look that had passed between her and some other man—the attitude of familiar confidence, if not of positive endearment.
When they were alone he called him "my boy," an endearment he never gave another.

senses: The head of a nunnery.
A dominatrix.
An ancient Roman lady.
ety: From Latin domina (“mistress”). Doublet of dame and donna.
examples: Each of the nuns was heard in her turn, while the others waited with the domina in the adjoining vestry.
A specific of the fem-dom, sub-male scene is that it is the segment with the highest presence of professional activity -- professional dominae abound.
I think that there is a reason why so many dominae are pro and paid: they don't get to do what they want. Maybe you talk to your pro dommes friends again and ask what they get out of it.

senses: The distance from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger used as an informal unit of length.
ety: From Middle English cubite, from Latin cubitum (“elbow, cubit”). Doublet of cubitus, covado, and codo.
examples: Which of you by taking thought can add one cubit unto his stature?

senses: Suffused with blushes or blushlike hues.
Embarrassed, blushing; feeling as though one might blush.
ety: From blush + -y.
examples: Well, before you have to ask and get all blushy again, I'll take you home, since you're so pathetically without wheels.
I felt my face do the melt, like Miss’s, only blushier.
I didn't feel blushy or quakey, but quite cool, and only a little excited.

senses: To eat or drink noisily.
To make a loud sucking noise.
ety: From Middle Dutch slurpen, slorpen (“to sip, slurp”), from Old Dutch *slurpan, from Proto-West Germanic *slurp- (“to sip, slurp”), perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *srebʰ-, *srobʰ- (“to sip, slurp, gulp”). Cognate with West Frisian sloarpe, sloarpje, slurvje (“to slurp”), German schlürfen (“to sip, slurp”), Swedish slurpa (“to slurp”), Norwegian slurpe (“to slurp”). Compare also Saterland Frisian slubberje (“to slurp”), German Low German slubbern (“to slurp”), Middle High German sluppern (“to slurp”), Swedish, Norwegian, and Icelandic slupra (“to slurp”), Middle High German sürfeln, sürpfeln (
examples: They sat in the kitchen slurping their spaghetti.

As the crowd cackles and caws, a white-backed vulture snakes its head deep into the wildebeest’s eye socket and hurriedly slurps, with grooved tongue, whatever it can before being ripped from its place at the table.
The mud slurped under our shoes.

senses: Sinful, villainous, criminal, or wicked, especially when noteworthy or notorious for such characteristics.
ety: From Latin nefārius (“execrable, abominable”), from nefās (“something contrary to divine law, an impious deed, sin, crime”), from ne- (“not”) + fās (“the dictates of religion, divine law”), which is related to Latin for (“to speak, to say”) and cognate to Ancient Greek φημί (phēmí, “to say”).
examples: Aliens have a nefarious connotation in many science fiction books.
The fact that the room was still in darkness made it obvious that something nefarious was afoot. Plainly there was dirty work in preparation at the cross-roads.

senses: A calypso musician.
ety: From calypso + -n- + -ian.
examples: The fourth and newest volume (subtitled “African Dreams and the Piccadilly High Life”) is scattered with calypsonians like Lord Kitchener, Young Growler and Young Tiger, and high-life bands like the African Messengers.

senses: One who confesses faith in Christianity in the face of persecution, but who is not martyred.
One who confesses to having done something wrong.
A priest who hears confession and then gives absolution.
Someone who acts as listener and helper.
ety: From Middle English confessor, confessour, from Anglo-Norman confessour, and its source, Latin cōnfessor, from cōnfiteor (“confess, admit, acknowledge”). By surface analysis, confess + -or.
examples: Long before Edward I, the English had a King Edward who they considered a martyr and a King Edward who they considered a confessor.

senses: A person, especially one who is famous or important.
A character (in a film, book, play, etc).
The creation of corporate persons named after living people.
Character represented; external appearance; persona.
ety: From Middle French personnage, from Old French personage; by surface analysis, person + -age (compare French suffix -age).
examples: The Matchmaking Festival provided social events for these lonely-hearted pilgrims, and allowed local personages to keep undesirables away from their daughters.

senses: A child's blanket.
ety: Baby-talk alteration of blanket. By surface analysis, clipping of blanket + -y.
examples: You sound like a little kid wrapped up in his banky watching his favorite t.v. show.
His banky, the grubby woollen blanket that he carried with him everywhere, was draped over the rest of his bedclothes.

senses: A person who practices the development of psychic ability.
A person who has extrasensory perception.
ety: From ESP + -er from ESP (“extrasensory perception”).
examples: I don't know why anybody would be spying on me, either, but—I'm neither a Lensman nor an esper, but I'd swear that somebody's peeking over my shoulder half the time.
But Espers can’t pick up any EK brain pattern farther than the horizon. It’s direct wave transmission. Even large objects cannot be penetrated. A building, say, or a—

senses: Any reptile of the order Crocodilia; a crocodile, alligator, caiman or gavial.
ety: From crocodile + -ian; compare translingual Crocodilia.
examples: Superb predators, the crocodilians are reptiles, and the only survivors of the archosaurs that included dinosaurs.
Crocodilians are essentially lizard-like in basic shape and are adapted to a largely aquatic life. ln water, they hunt and eat their prey and advertise their size and location by bellowing.
However, it is possible that baby titanoboas and Titanoboa eggs were preyed upon by the same crocodilians the adults ate.

senses: A dish consisting of French fries topped with cheese curds and gravy, eaten primarily in Canada.
Chiefly with a qualifying word: any of a number of variations on the basic poutine dish.
ety: Borrowed from Canadian French poutine (“French fries with cheese curds and gravy; any of various kinds of pudding”); further etymology uncertain, possibly either: * a variant of French pouding (“pudding”), borrowed from English pudding (possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰew- (“to swell”)); or * from a dialectal French word influenced by French pouding or English pudding, though this word has not been identified. The Canadian French word is generally thought to have been coined by the Canadian restaurateur Fernand Lachance (1918–2004) as a name for the dish which is said to have be
examples: Jean made an eight-hour trip across the border into Quebec just to satisfy his craving for poutine.
In Italian poutine, gravy is replaced with spaghetti sauce.

senses: A grain of barley.
A small groove between two moldings.
ety: From barley + corn.
examples: The Town Mouse came, and they sat down to a dinner of barleycorns and roots, the latter of which had a distinctly earthy flavour.

senses: To cook (something) in simmering or very hot liquid (usually water; sometimes wine, broth, or otherwise).
To be cooked in such manner.
ety: From Middle English pochen (“to poach (eggs)”), from Old French pocher "to put (egg yolks) in pockets" (i.e. in bags formed by the whites), from Old French poche (“pocket”).
examples: Eldridge closed the despatch-case with a snap and, rising briskly, walked down the corridor to his solitary table in the dining-car. Mulligatawny soup, poached turbot, roast leg of lamb—the usual railway dinner.

senses: A drink or dessert (especially ice cream) topped with espresso and sometimes a caramel or chocolate sauce.
ety: Borrowed from Italian affogato (literally “drowned”).
examples: The magic of affogato is that you get two pleasures in one: a spoonable dessert sauced with coffee, and a cream-blushed drink to chase it.

senses: The butchering of meat.
A butcher's shop; a meat market.
The cruel, ruthless killings of humans, as if at a slaughterhouse.
A disastrous effort, an atrocious failure.
Surgery that was botched or is asserted by the speaker to have been so.
ety: From Middle English bocherie, from Old French. See butcher for more.
examples: The tyrannous and bloody act is done,— The most arch deed of piteous massacre That ever yet this land was guilty of. Dighton and Forrest, who I did suborn To do this piece of ruthless butchery

senses: Something which is free; a giveaway or handout.
ety: From free + -b- (epenthetic) + -ie or free + -bie.
examples: I didn't buy a thing, but they were handing out some neat freebies and samples.
I had seen its first show when it was a freebie, but I thought it made multiples in general look silly – no one changes clothes THAT much!

senses: Similar or comparable to a prince.
Befitting a prince.
ety: From Middle English princely, pryncely, equivalent to prince + -ly (adjectival suffix). Compare Dutch prinselijk.
examples: No expense was spared in making it a princely residence.

senses: A midstrength, traditional Belgian and Flemish sour beer of spontaneous fermentation.
ety: Borrowed from French lambic, from Belgian Dutch lambiek, from French alambic, from Old French alambic, from Medieval Latin alembīcum, from Arabic الْإِنْبِيق (al-ʔinbīq), borrowed from Ancient Greek ἄμβιξ (ámbix). Doublet of alembic and ambix.
examples: Wooden casks serve a special role in the maturation of lambic by allowing a little oxygen to slowly contact the beer.

senses: Nervous and excited.
Tending to jump; full of jumps.
ety: From jump + -y.
examples: We moved at a good clip, so I reached up to pull shut the window coverings, just in case this jumpy frog decided to escape.
Meanwhile, the car pursued its jumpy course, and I could not prevent myself laughing.

senses: Characteristic of common folk.
Informal, affable, and familiar.
ety: From folks + -y or folk + -sy.
examples: Mr. Clooney, as a veteran spacewalker, with his resonant voice and folksy yarns, seems to be channeling every imperturbable astronaut you ever heard speaking from on high.

senses: Anything held allodially.
ety: From Middle French allodial, and its source, Latin allōdiālis (“held in freehold”), from allōdium.
examples: Charles Theodore, elector Palatine, was generally considered as rightful heir to all the Bavarian territories which were not female fiefs or allodials.

senses: Experiencing discontent, dissatisfaction.
ety: From dis- + contented.
examples: After her injury, Alice was a discontented woman.

senses: A dish made of raw fish or seafood.
ety: Borrowed from Italian crudo (literally “raw”). Doublet of crude.
examples: Food, like fashion, has a brutally short trend cycle, as the trickle-down from San Sebastián to Smith Street takes barely a season. So, this year's crudo could be next year's tuna carpaccio.
Then, a few years back, poke started appearing on stray restaurant menus, sometimes identified as Hawaiian crudo or ceviche.

senses: Like (that of) a girl; feminine.
ety: From girl + -ish.
examples: She saw her own face, glowing with girlish beauty, and illuminating all the interior of the dusky mirror in which she had been wont to gaze at it.
Three little maids from school are we, / Pert as a school-girl well can be, / Filled to the brim with girlish glee, / Three little maids from school!
April, April, / Laugh thy girlish laughter; / Then, the moment after, / Weep thy girlish tears!

senses: Showing the qualities of a friendly and helpful neighbour.
ety: From neighbour + -ly.
examples: She's so neighbourly that she always holds a welcoming party for new residents.
I got the impression you were looking for something, and it crossed my mind to ask you what that might be. Just being friendly, sir, just being neighbourly.

senses: A clay brick.
ety: From Fletton, Cambridgeshire, England, where originally manufactured.
examples: Pooley's eyes suddenly alighted upon a half empty bag of cement which lay among a few unused red flettons in the corner of the patio.

senses: An Indonesian food made from partially-cooked soybeans fermented by a fungus (either Rhizopus oligosporus or Rhizopus oryzae).
ety: From Indonesian tempe, from Malay tempe, possibly from Old Javanese tumpi (“a food made from starch and tempeh”), or Malay tapai (“fermentation”).
examples: Usually sporulation occurred when the tempeh had been exposed to air ( e.g. as the result of uncovering of the pan too frequently ) .
The leaves were of use only to the tempeh factories, which collected them every night.

senses: A celebrity; a famous person, a one who is celebrated.
ety: Clipping of celebrity.
examples: Just in case you thought celebs stay famous on their own, think again. There's a whole pack of people who help a star each day
